name: Urine face washing

lead: Urine has a long history of cosmetic and household uses. In ancient Rome it was used to whiten teeth and, fermented, to clean cloth, and today some urine-therapy followers rub it on the skin hoping for a clearer, smoother complexion.

Believers point to its urea content: synthetic urea is a common moisturiser ingredient. Reference sources note that real urine is too dilute for that effect, and no published study has tested urine as a face wash.

paras: Practitioners of urine therapy describe applying their own urine to the skin or rinsing the face with it; details vary by tradition and are not given here.
Reference sources state there is no scientific evidence supporting therapeutic use of untreated urine. Skin irritation and infection are possible, and urine can carry bacteria or medication residues.

angle.text: Followers apply urine hoping its urea softens and clears the skin. The idea echoes the historical use of urine for cleaning and whitening in antiquity.

lead: Urine face washing refers to the use of urine as a cleanser or complexion treatment. It belongs to the broader tradition of urine therapy, which includes rubbing urine on the skin or gums.[1]

Historical precedent is mostly dental and household: ancient Romans used urine to whiten teeth, and fermented urine to launder cloth and remove grease stains.[2] The Roman poet Catullus mocked the Spanish practice of cleaning teeth with urine.[3]

Proponents argue that urea, which makes up about 9.3 g per litre of urine, is a known skin conditioner. Commercial urea creams use synthetic urea at concentrations far higher than urine provides.[1] No published study has tested urine as a facial wash.

paras: Classical antiquity used fermented urine (lant) to wash cloth, and Roman dentists and others used it for teeth whitening.[2][1] Catullus ridicules a Celtiberian man for polishing his teeth with urine.[3]
Urea acts as a humectant and keratolytic at high concentrations, but urine is too dilute for that effect, and there is no scientific evidence supporting therapeutic use of untreated urine.[1]
